title: Guiding Question
notes: Open with the central problem: topology produces loops, but computation needs a finite algebraic record. The appendix explains how to move from a geometric generating set to formal words, then to a quotient where selected loops become trivial. Keep the emphasis on reading a presentation as instructions rather than as a black-box group name.

title: Presentations From Topology
notes: Connect the algebra to cell and loop pictures. Edges or named loops contribute generators, while faces, glued boundaries, or homotopies contribute words that must close up. The slide should make clear that a presentation is not decoration around a group; it is a compact record of the topology that produced the group.

title: Free Word Machine
notes: Treat the free group as a deterministic normal-form machine. In a free group there are no hidden relations, so the only automatic simplification is adjacent inverse cancellation. The stack image from the notebook makes the rule inspectable: read left to right, push a letter, and pop only when the next letter is its inverse.

title: Reduction Trace
notes: Walk the table as an execution trace rather than a proof by assertion. The word abBAcCaaBAb first cancels bB, then aA, then cC, leaving aaBAb. The idempotence check matters pedagogically: once a word is reduced, running the reduction machine again should not change it.

title: Presentation Quotient
notes: Now add relations. Start with F(X), map a free word to the group element it names, and collect the words that map to the identity. Because quotients require a normal subgroup, the relation set R really means its normal closure. This is the algebraic bridge from free syntax to the target group.

title: Dihedral Normal Forms
notes: Use the dihedral presentation as the main finite laboratory. The relations x^5, y^2, and (xy)^2 force a ten-element model with five rotations and five reflected states. The rewrite examples are chosen to show preservation of action: different raw words can collapse to the same normal form without changing the represented symmetry.

title: Relations As Closed Paths
notes: Read a relation as a closed walk in the Cayley graph. If x^5 is a relation, following five x-edges returns to the starting vertex. If (xy)^2 is a relation, the alternating square also closes. This visual criterion is useful because a failed closure immediately exposes a broken presentation model.

title: Normal Closure
notes: Stress why conjugates appear. A quotient should make a relation loop vanish no matter where the basepoint has been moved, so g r g^{-1} must also be trivial. The notebook check tests this by moving a relation loop around the dihedral Cayley graph and verifying closure at every sampled vertex.

title: Schreier-Style Action
notes: Shift from the full Cayley graph to an action graph. The pentagon keeps orbit points rather than all group elements, so x acts as a five-cycle while y acts as an involution. This is a useful lower-dimensional inspection: the presentation relations must still act trivially on the orbit even though the graph has fewer vertices.

title: Free Products
notes: Introduce free products as the same word philosophy with factor groups as alphabets. A reduced word alternates nonidentity pieces from G and H; if two adjacent pieces come from the same factor, first multiply them inside that factor. The tree artifact shows how quickly alternating normal forms branch.

title: Free Product Failure Mode
notes: Use the failure cases to prevent a common mistake. Juxtaposition alone is not a normal form when adjacent letters live in the same factor. The CSV examples show reductions such as s s r becoming r and r r r s becoming s, while an already alternating word stays unchanged under the reducer.

title: Abelianized Shadow
notes: Abelianization is a deliberately lossy inspection. Replace each relation word by exponent sums in the generators and compute the rank of the resulting integer relation matrix. This cannot identify the whole group, but it quickly detects what survives after all commutators have been forced to vanish.

title: Universal Properties
notes: Close the algebra with the two universal mapping properties stated in the source span. A free group is the unique extension machine for functions defined on its generators. A free product is the unique extension machine for homomorphisms from its two factors. These are characterization principles, not extra examples.

title: Recap Checklist
notes: Use the final slide as an instructor checklist. Students should leave able to reduce free words, interpret a presentation as a quotient by normal closure, test relations on Cayley or action graphs, recognize alternating normal forms in free products, and use abelianization as a quick consistency check rather than a complete invariant.
